memoryText: Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jeremiah 17:7-8 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jeremiah wrote these words in a land of drought, to a people who were trusting in everything but God. It is a promise that holds in hard seasons.

“Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD.” The word “blessed” means deeply happy, in a good place. The Bible links this blessing not to circumstances but to trust. And the trust is placed in a person: “whose trust is the LORD.” He himself is the trust. It is not trust in a technique, a doctrine as such, or a strategy for success. It is a relationship with a person.

“He is like a tree planted by water.” The picture is of a tree whose roots go to the stream. In a dry country, the tree by the water has a source that does not depend on rainfall. The roots do the hidden work, “sending out” toward the water. So much of the Christian life is hidden roots: time in prayer, reading Scripture, quiet obedience, worship.

“Does not fear when heat comes.” Notice that heat does come. The blessed person is not spared the heat. But they do not fear it, because the roots are in the stream. The next verse adds, “Its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.” In the drought it keeps bearing fruit.

Contrast the previous verses: the person who trusts in man is a shrub in the desert. The difference is not in the climate but in the source. Say this verse and ask where your roots are going this week.
weekInReview: This week you stood in the temple gate with Jeremiah and heard the sermon that said a building cannot save you. You read the great questions: “Is there no balm in Gilead?” and the invitation to boast only in knowing the LORD. You prayed Psalms 79 and 85, a lament over the ruined city and a prayer for revival in which steadfast love and faithfulness meet. You read Jeremiah’s mockery of idols, his own struggle when the wicked prosper, and the ruined loincloth. You read the deceitful heart and the two trees. You watched the potter, the shattered jar, and Jeremiah in the stocks, burning with the word he could not hold in. The week taught that God’s patience has limits, that religion without obedience is empty, and that the one who trusts in the LORD is like a tree by the stream.
reflectionQuestions: Jeremiah warned people not to trust in the temple as a charm. What “temple of the LORD” slogan might you be leaning on instead of obedience?
Jeremiah’s prayers are honest, even angry. What do you need to bring honestly to God that you have been holding back?
The blessed man in Jeremiah 17 is like a tree planted by water. What are the “roots” you are sending out each week, and where might they be shallow?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you send roots deep into him.
Tell him how you want to trust him in heat and drought.
Thank Jesus in whom you are blessed.
